title: How are you handling discontinued voltage regulators and other EOL semiconductors in 2026?
text:
K

kieuuu
New member

Curious how the community is managing this in 2026 — it's been hitting our projects a lot harder over the last 12 months.

Most of what we work on is small-to-mid volume industrial and embedded hardware (1k–50k units/year). EOL pressure on basic components has gotten noticeably worse since 2024. The categories keep repeating themselves:

LDO and linear regulators: Older TI, Linear Tech (now ADI), and National Semi parts that went NRND years ago but still ship in millions of legacy boards.

PMICs paired with older SoCs: Once the SoC vendor drops software support, the PMIC usually disappears within a quarter or two.

Small-package discretes (SOT-23, SC-70): Long lead times even when not officially EOL.

A recent example: A TI TPS7A4501 going NRND for a client that's had it in production since 2018. We've been sourcing it through a mix of authorized and open-market channels. Quotes are ranging 2x to 6x original price depending on lot size and traceability requirements — turned what should have been a routine order into a 6-week scramble to keep a $200k PO moving.
Discussion Questions​
For regulated or mission-critical products (medical, industrial, automotive) — are you still redesigning around an EOL part, or accepting the obsolescence premium? The cost-vs-carriage trade has shifted noticeably for us and I'm not sure what's "normal" anymore.

How much do you trust independent distributors these days? We've been testing every incoming lot (decaps, electrical, sometimes X-ray) because the counterfeit problem hasn't gone away. Curious how smaller teams without that capability are managing.

When an urgent EOL lands on your desk — what's your actual workflow? Authorized franchise first? Internal allocation? Brokers? Different channels keep getting recommended to us and I'd like to know what's actually working in practice.
